title: Patent Search Tools: An Unranked Shortlist by Job (2026)
summary: Compare nine patent search tools by the research job they support, with current access details, workflow boundaries, and legal scope for prior art work.
body_markdown:
A patent search can start from a publication number, claim limitation, product, technical drawing, or invention disclosure. The right tool depends on what must happen next. A quick lookup, international family review, invalidity search, and portfolio landscape require different sources, controls, and outputs. The shortlist below maps nine tools to those jobs and makes the important legal and workflow boundaries visible.


## How we built this unranked shortlist


We at &AI publish this comparison, and it includes our own product. This is a desk-researched comparison based on official public and vendor materials reviewed on October 5, 2026. We did not conduct hands-on trials, benchmark retrieval performance, or test every plan and feature entitlement. The shortlist is unranked, and the order follows research jobs rather than product quality.


The candidate set covers nine established options that illustrate the main categories a patent team is likely to evaluate: free public databases, international family and Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) resources, patent-to-scholar research, commercial semantic search, enriched patent data, portfolio intelligence, and a patent litigation workspace. It is not an exhaustive market census. We excluded drafting, prosecution docketing, annuity, and general court-analytics systems whose primary job is not patent searching.


We compared each option against five practical questions:


- **Source fit:** Can it retrieve the patent documents, non-patent literature (NPL), product evidence, or legal data the assignment requires?
- **Search control:** Does it support the relevant field, Boolean, proximity, classification, date, family, semantic, or image inputs?
- **Review context:** Does it expose supporting passages, citations, family relationships, dates, or legal events?
- **Downstream work:** Can the team preserve results and carry selected evidence into the required analysis or deliverable?
- **Access:** Is it public, account-gated, trial-based, licensed, or subject to plan-specific entitlements?


## Key takeaways


- **Shortlist our workspace when litigation evidence must feed attorney-controlled work product.** We search patent publications and NPL, use ClinicalTrials.gov as a separate source, discover publicly available product materials on the live web, and chart product documents you supply, including archived pages you captured. Selected evidence can then move into invalidity analysis and claim-chart work.
- **Google Patents is a useful free first pass.** United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) Patent Public Search adds exact U.S. field, set, and proximity searching.
- **Espacenet and PATENTSCOPE answer different international questions.** Espacenet is useful for families and legal events. PATENTSCOPE centers published Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) applications and multilingual searching.
- **The Lens Patent Search connects patents with scholarly works.** Its PatSeq facility is a separate set of biological-sequence tools.
- **IPRally, Derwent Patent Search, and Patsnap Analytics support specialized commercial research.** IPRally combines semantic retrieval with automated patent review. Derwent adds human-enriched records. Patsnap Analytics combines several patent and literature search modes with legal data, workspaces, monitoring, landscapes, and reports.
- **Search scope must follow the legal question.** America Invents Act (AIA) 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1) has several distinct routes to prior art. Inter partes review (IPR) grounds are narrower because 35 U.S.C. § 311(b) limits them to patents and printed publications.


## What separates a patent search tool from a patent database?


A patent database stores and retrieves patent records. A search tool can add query construction, semantic ranking, classification search, patent-family grouping, citations, legal events, annotations, monitoring, analytics, collaboration, and downstream work product.


Source coverage matters as much as interface quality. The USPTO's Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP) § 904 identifies U.S. patent documents, foreign patent documents, and NPL as distinct sources examiners may need to search. That[examiner-search guidance](https://www.uspto.gov/web/offices/pac/mpep/s904.html) is useful for source planning, but it does not define every legally available route under § 102. The detailed legal-scope section below addresses those routes and their different date questions.

Our AI workspace for patent litigation is built for the point where retrieval becomes invalidity work.[Prior Art Search](https://www.tryandai.com/product/prior-art-search) can start from a patent number, full claim, specific limitation, plain-English technical description, or patent figure. Our current public materials list patent applications and publications from the United States, Europe, Japan, WIPO, Korea, China, Great Britain, and Germany.


Our NPL search includes research papers, journals, and technical standards. ClinicalTrials.gov is a separate source. For product evidence, we discover publicly available materials on the live web, such as product pages, specifications, manuals, teardowns, reviews, and marketing materials.


We can also chart product documents you supply, including archived pages you have captured. We do not describe that workflow as independent retrieval of historical web captures.


Each result identifies the passage or figure supporting the match. Attorneys can refine the search, decide which references matter, and move selected evidence into[Invalidity Analysis](https://www.tryandai.com/product/invalidity-analysis) or a limitation-by-limitation[claim chart](https://www.tryandai.com/product/claim-charts) . Attorneys remain responsible for the cutoff date, priority entitlement, prior art status, combinations, and final work product.


Our[current pricing](https://www.tryandai.com/pricing) is credit-based. The public page lists pay as you go at $0.40 per credit. Monthly Pro is $625 per user and includes 2,500 monthly credits, with additional credits at $0.25 each.


Over the 90 days measured as of July 2026, a prior art search averaged 176 credits, equal to $70.40 at the pay-as-you-go rate, $44 at the monthly Pro rate, or $35.20 at the annual Pro rate. Those are dated averages, not fixed search prices. Actual usage varies with patent length, requested results, and search configuration. Our[current self-serve terms](https://www.tryandai.com/terms) require a valid payment method and end a trial on the earlier of seven days or depletion of the trial credits. The applicable signup page controls any stated credit allotment, so we do not state a number here. Self-serve access is available to verified patent practitioners and other approved professional users and organizations, subject to our eligibility review and approval.


**Shortlist us when:** Your patent litigation team needs to take source-linked search evidence into attorney-controlled invalidity analysis and claim-chart work in the same workspace.


**Boundary:** We focus on enforcement and defense. Patent drafting, prosecution docketing, annuity management, and general court analytics belong in other systems.


## For fast free retrieval: Google Patents


Google Patents is a low-friction choice for retrieving a known publication, learning the vocabulary of a technology, or building an initial citation trail. It covers more than 120 million publications from over 100 patent offices, plus technical documents and books from Google Scholar, Google Books, and the Prior Art Archive. Google warns that it[does not guarantee complete coverage](https://support.google.com/faqs/answer/7049585?hl=en&ref_topic=6390989) .


The interface accepts numbers, free text, exact phrases, metadata fields, Cooperative Patent Classification (CPC) codes, Boolean logic, and chemistry queries. A long block of text can feed the Prior Art Finder keyword extractor. Google’s[search syntax guide](https://support.google.com/faqs/answer/7049475?hl=en) also makes an important distinction: proximity operators affect ranking, rather than determining whether a document is retrieved.


Google removes all but the highest-ranking member of each simple patent family from the result list. In this context, a simple family means documents sharing the same set of priority claims. That is deduplication of the displayed list, not a complete extended-family analysis. The[results documentation](https://support.google.com/faqs/answer/7049588?hl=en) also says the hit count is approximate and that users can export up to the top 1,000 results as CSV.


The query remains visible for recording, and a team can preserve its query and CSV output. Google Patents does not provide the matter-level search history, review decisions, or claim-element mapping of a litigation workspace.


**Fit:** Known-document retrieval, terminology discovery, citation chasing, and preliminary searching.


## For precise U.S. queries: USPTO Patent Public Search


Patent Public Search is the USPTO’s free system for issued U.S. patents and published U.S. applications. Basic Search handles a known number, keywords, and common fields. Advanced Search supports field codes, Boolean logic, wildcards, and proximity operators.


The operator meanings deserve attention.` WITHn` searches within a specified number of sentences, while` SAMEn` searches within paragraphs.` ADJn` and` NEARn` operate at the term level within a sentence. The USPTO publishes the current definitions in its[operator reference](https://www.uspto.gov/patents/search/patent-public-search/operators) .


Advanced Search assigns each query an` L` set number and lists those sets in Search History, so a searcher can combine earlier result sets. The enhanced layout adds tagged documents, notes, and hit-term panels. Search-result columns can be copied or exported, and the main research panes can be printed.


Those controls apply within the current session. Patent Public Search cannot save a workspace, notes disappear when the session ends, and the workspace times out after 30 minutes of inactivity following a two-minute warning. The USPTO’s[interface FAQ](https://www.uspto.gov/patents/search/patent-public-search/faqs) documents each limit. For a reproducible record, export or print the needed search history and results before ending the session.


**Fit:** Authoritative U.S. document retrieval and reproducible field, set, and proximity searches.


**Boundary:** Its corpus centers U.S. patent documents. A complete assignment may still require foreign collections, NPL, product evidence, or other § 102 categories.


## For worldwide families and legal events: Espacenet


The European Patent Office (EPO)’s Espacenet provides free access to data on more than 150 million patent documents and updates the service daily. It supports Smart search, advanced fields, Boolean and proximity logic, CPC and International Patent Classification (IPC) exploration, machine translation, citations, simple and extended family views, and legal events. The[EPO’s Espacenet overview](https://www.epo.org/en/searching-for-patents/technical/espacenet) gives the coverage figure and documents its links to Global Dossier and the Common Citation Document.


Espacenet is especially useful after another tool surfaces a promising reference. A searcher can inspect related filings, compare publication stages, follow cited and citing documents, and review reported events across family members. Classification search helps when the art uses terminology that differs from the claim.


Legal-event data is a lead for further analysis. The EPO notes that accuracy and timing depend on the national offices supplying the data, with delays varying by country and period. Its[legal-status caveat](https://www.epo.org/en/service-support/faq/searching-patents/espacenet-worldwide-patent-search/how-date-legal-status) is a reason to use the appropriate national register for a dispositive status conclusion.


**Fit:** International family expansion, classification research, translation, and legal-event context.


## For PCT and multilingual searching: PATENTSCOPE


WIPO’s PATENTSCOPE provides full-text international PCT applications on publication day and includes participating national and regional collections. Search modes include fields, Boolean and proximity operators, IPC, cross-lingual expansion, NPL, and exact or substructure chemical searching.


The July 2026 AI-Assisted Search release converts natural-language instructions into structured PATENTSCOPE queries. Version 1.0 focuses on keywords, publication dates, and country codes. Applicant, assignee, standard-essential patent, and patent-number queries remain planned enhancements. WIPO hosts the model on its own premises and describes the current scope in the[release announcement](https://www.wipo.int/en/web/patentscope/w/news/2026/patentscope-ai-assisted-search-now-available) .


Basic patent searching does not require an account. A free WIPO account is required for AI-Assisted Search and chemical-structure search. An account also enables saved queries and settings, along with result downloads up to 10,000 records, as the[PATENTSCOPE FAQ](https://www.wipo.int/en/web/patentscope/faqs_patentscope) explains.


**Fit:** PCT research, multilingual discovery, cross-lingual query expansion, and chemistry-related searching.


## For patents and scholarship in one research graph: The Lens Patent Search


The Lens Patent Search combines global patent records with scholarly works and citation links between the two collections. Its patent interface supports Boolean and structured fields, classifications, filters, family grouping, collections, annotations, exports, and analysis dashboards. Reversible patent-to-scholar links let a researcher move from a patent to cited papers and then identify later patents that cite a scholarly work.


Biological sequence search is a separate facility. PatSeq includes tools for sequence data, genome exploration, locus analysis, Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLAST) similarity searching, and text searching within patents that disclose sequences. The Lens[patent-search tutorial](https://support.lens.org/knowledge-base/patent-search-analysis/) distinguishes ordinary Patent Search from the PatSeq tools.


Public access does not mean unrestricted commercial use. The Lens terms grant ordinary platform access for personal, noncommercial use. Commercial use, institutional access, application programming interfaces (APIs), custom services, and bulk data can require separate agreements or fees. Those limits are set out in the[Lens terms](https://about.lens.org/policies/) .


**Fit:** Patent-to-paper citation tracing, academic and policy research, life-sciences investigation, and technology mapping.


## For semantic patent discovery and automated review: IPRally


The current[IPRally Search](https://www.iprally.com/patent-search) product combines its examiner-citation-trained Graph AI model with free-text, publication-number, Boolean, claim, document, and image inputs. Smart Search accepts combinations of free text, plain-text files, PDFs, Microsoft Office files, and common image formats. It interprets the supplied material, creates an editable claim-style query, and returns patent results for review. The[current Smart Search guide](https://help.iprally.com/en/articles/13104548-smart-search) says it replaced the earlier standalone Image Search in December 2025.


The Invalidity Search Agent adds an automated workflow for a granted patent or published application. The user supplies a publication number, selects claims, and sets the cutoff date. The Agent extracts claim features, searches using the claims, family members, and examiner citations, then expands from citations of highly relevant hits. It reviews candidates in batches and creates an interactive Feature Chart.


Outputs include claim-feature findings with paragraph citations, relevance tiers, an editable IPRally project, and a written report addressing novelty and inventive step. For U.S. patents, the report frames its analysis under §§ 102 and 103. Feature charts can be exported to XLSX, PDF, or DOCX, and the evidence package can include selected patent PDFs. IPRally’s[Invalidity Agent documentation](https://help.iprally.com/en/articles/16349726-invalidity-search-agent) also states that the Agent takes the asserted priority date as given. It does not determine whether the target is entitled to that date.


IPRally's[current pricing page](https://www.iprally.com/pricing) lists annual Single user, Team, and Enterprise plans and does not publish seat prices. Formal evaluation trials are available at IPRally's discretion. Agents are annual entitlements on Team or Enterprise plans, and Pro users receive limited trial runs each month.


**Fit:** Patent-focused semantic discovery, automated feature review, monitoring, classification, and structured invalidity reports.


**Boundary:** The search pool is patent literature. Matters that depend on standards, manuals, product activity, or other NPL require additional source research. The generated report requires independent professional review.


## For human-enriched patent records: Derwent Patent Search


Derwent Patent Search is the current name for the product formerly called Derwent Innovation, as Clarivate's[current Derwent product page](https://clarivate.com/intellectual-property/derwent/patent-search/) confirms. It combines global patent records with the Derwent World Patents Index (DWPI). Subject-matter specialists create English titles and abstracts organized around an invention's novelty, use, and advantage. The[current DWPI overview](https://clarivate.com/intellectual-property/derwent/world-patents-index/) also documents standardized indexing, corrected bibliographic data, and invention-family grouping.


The platform combines natural-language AI search with Boolean, field, classification, proximity, and citation strategies. Its current product materials describe more than 300 searchable fields, search-combination controls, invention-family citations, litigation context, and scientific literature from Web of Science. Those features support complex, repeatable professional research, while the human-authored DWPI summaries reduce initial review time.


Access is commercial. Clarivate does not publish a list price and offers[trial access by request](https://clarivate.com/intellectual-property/derwent/) .


**Fit:** Patent departments and search professionals that value curated English summaries, normalized assignee and family data, and complex repeatable queries.


**Boundary:** Derwent Patent Search is a broad professional research environment. Litigation teams may still need a separate workflow for claim-specific legal analysis, contentions, and firm-formatted claim charts.


## For patent search and portfolio intelligence: Patsnap Analytics


Patsnap Analytics provides several distinct routes into its patent data. The[current Analytics plan comparison](https://www.patsnap.com/pricing) lists Simple and Field Search, Expert Search, Semantic Search, Bulk Search, Classification Search, Image Search, Literature Search, Legal Search, and separate publication and family modes. Bulk search matches lists of publication or application numbers and assignees. Semantic search starts from a technical disclosure or patent number, while Classification search follows CPC, IPC, and Patsnap taxonomies. Family mode searches and displays families as the unit of review rather than merely grouping a publication-level result set.


Its separate[Image Search](https://help.patsnap.com/hc/en-us/articles/115000937409-What-is-Image-Search-How-Can-I-Search-for-Design-Patents-And-Utility-Models-Within-Patsnap) compares visual features across design patents, registered design rights, and utility models. This retrieves visually similar documents; claim-element analysis still requires review of the claims and technical disclosure. Semantic search can return patents and scientific literature when literature is included. The current plan comparison describes Legal Search for litigation, re-examination or invalidation, licensing, assignment, and pledge data.


Results can move into shared Workspaces for folders, comments, custom fields, review tracking, and alerts, as Patsnap's[current Workspace guide](https://help.patsnap.com/hc/en-us/articles/35174449698717-Workspaces) explains.[Hiro Bulk Ask](https://help.patsnap.com/hc/en-us/articles/28581398723869-Hiro-Bulk-Ask) applies the same question to a selected patent set and can export answer tags and supporting snippets or save them back to a Workspace. Monitoring, citation analysis, dashboards, landscapes, portfolio comparisons, and reports support ongoing work on filing trends, technology clusters, assignee activity, legal events, and competitive movement.


This assessment is limited to Patsnap Analytics. Patsnap Eureka agents, Bio, Chemical, Synapse, and Open Platform are separate products or modules with different data and workflows. Capabilities from those products should not be attributed to Analytics without confirming the applicable subscription.


Analytics is sold in Standard and Premium editions. The public plan page compares their feature entitlements but does not state an Analytics list price.


**Fit:** Enterprise patent and scientific-literature research, legal and litigation analysis, shared patent review, monitoring, competitive landscapes, and portfolio reporting.


**Boundary:** Portfolio-scale analysis and a litigation-ready claim chart are different outputs. A litigation team still needs a controlled path from a selected reference to claim-specific evidence and legal analysis.


## Build your shortlist around the research job


Start with the decision the work must support. These are job matches, not rankings:


- **Known patent or quick technology scan:** Shortlist Google Patents.
- **Exact U.S. field, set, or proximity query:** Shortlist Patent Public Search.
- **Worldwide family and legal-event research:** Shortlist Espacenet.
- **Published PCT applications, multilingual terms, or chemical structures:** Shortlist PATENTSCOPE.
- **Patent and scholarly citations in one dataset:** Shortlist The Lens Patent Search.
- **Patent-focused semantic discovery and automated invalidity review:** Shortlist IPRally.
- **Human-enriched professional search records:** Shortlist Derwent Patent Search.
- **Patent, literature, legal, and portfolio intelligence:** Shortlist Patsnap Analytics.
- **Invalidity search through attorney-controlled analysis and claim-chart work:** Shortlist our workspace.


Cost follows the job. Free public tools can handle document retrieval and many preliminary searches. Commercial platforms earn their place when semantic retrieval, normalized data, saved work, monitoring, collaboration, or analytics reduce repeated effort. A litigation workspace earns its place when the deliverable is an invalidity position or claim chart rather than a list of references.


## A defensible patent search starts with the legal scope


No query proves that every relevant reference has been found. Search quality comes from correct scope, multiple retrieval modes, iteration, and a reviewable record.


1. **Define the proceeding and jurisdiction.** Patentability, district-court invalidity, IPR, freedom to operate (FTO), and landscaping ask different questions. FTO focuses on potentially enforceable claims in the jurisdictions where the planned activity will occur. A global family list does not answer that question by itself.
2. **Identify the governing version of § 102 before setting a cutoff.** AIA §§ 102 and 103 generally apply when an application contains or ever contained a claim with an effective filing date on or after March 16, 2013. Some applications filed later remain under pre-AIA law, and transition applications require closer review. The USPTO’s[applicability-date guidance](https://www.uspto.gov/web/offices/pac/mpep/s2159.html) explains the transition rules. Under the AIA, the effective filing date is claim-specific and depends on the earliest priority or benefit date to which that claimed invention is actually entitled. The first date in a family tree is an input, not an automatic conclusion.
3. **Match the evidence to the statutory route.** AIA § 102(a)(1) separately asks whether the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before its effective filing date, subject to § 102(b)(1). The applicable event date differs by route: ordinarily the grant date for a public patent, the public-accessibility date for a printed publication, the qualifying use date, the qualifying sale or offer date, or the date the subject matter became publicly available under the residual clause. The on-sale category is not controlled by a general public-disclosure requirement. In *Helsinn Healthcare S.A. v. Teva Pharmaceuticals USA, Inc.* , the[Supreme Court held](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/18pdf/586us1r10_fcgk.pdf) that a sale to a third party obligated to keep the invention confidential can qualify as prior art. Section 102(a)(2) supplies a separate route for certain U.S. patents, U.S. patent application publications, and WIPO-published PCT applications designating the United States that name another inventor and were effectively filed before the claimed invention, even when publication occurs later, subject to §§ 102(b)(2) and 102(d).
4. **Limit IPR grounds correctly.** An IPR petition may raise only §§ 102 or 103 grounds based on patents or printed publications under[35 U.S.C. § 311(b)](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid%3AUSC-prelim-title35-section311&num=0&edition=prelim) . Product use, sale activity, or physical evidence may matter in district court, but it cannot serve as the independent basis of an IPR ground unless the relevant disclosure is established through a qualifying patent or printed publication.
5. **Prove the event and date required by the asserted route.** A date printed on a manual, web page, video, or slide deck does not automatically prove when a printed publication became accessible to the interested public. The USPTO’s[printed-publication guidance](https://www.uspto.gov/web/offices/pac/mpep/s2128.html) treats public accessibility as a fact-specific inquiry. A public-use or on-sale theory calls for evidence of the use or transaction and its timing. A later document may corroborate an earlier event, but its later date does not by itself establish when that event occurred.
6. **Search by concept, then regain precision.** Claim, description, and image search can surface unfamiliar language. Turn the resulting synonyms, CPC or IPC codes, inventors, assignees, citations, and dates into Boolean, fielded, and classification queries.
7. **Expand families, citations, and sources.** Review earlier family members, backward and forward citations, examiner references, prosecution history, papers, standards, manuals, archived pages, and other evidence allowed by the assignment.
8. **Preserve what a reviewer could reproduce.** Keep the database, query, date, filters, cut-off, result count, family setting, narrowing steps, reviewed range, and supporting passages.


That record matters when IPR estoppel is disputed. After a final written decision,[§ 315(e)(2)](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid%3AUSC-prelim-title35-section315&num=0&edition=prelim) can bar the petitioner, its real party in interest, or its privy from asserting in a civil action or International Trade Commission proceeding that a claim is invalid on a ground the petitioner raised or reasonably could have raised during that IPR. In June 2026, *Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corp.* rejected hindsight-tainted evidence and held that a classification search returning an unreviewable mass of results needs more evidence to establish discoverability. The court also reiterated that estoppel speaks in terms of grounds, not isolated references. The[Federal Circuit opinion](https://www.cafc.uscourts.gov/opinions-orders/24-2088.OPINION.6-18-2026_2711717.pdf) and our analysis of the[skilled-searcher standard](https://www.tryandai.com/blog/ironburg-valve-skilled-searcher-ipr-estoppel) explain why a timestamped search record should capture the final query, narrowing steps, and review range.


Every tool also has a timing blind spot. U.S. nonprovisional utility and plant applications generally publish around 18 months after the earliest filing date for which a benefit is sought, subject to exceptions in[35 U.S.C. § 122](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid%3AUSC-prelim-title35-section122&num=0&edition=prelim) . An unpublished application itself cannot appear in a public patent search. If it later publishes or issues, it may qualify under § 102(a)(2) from an earlier effective-filing date when the statute’s requirements are met.


## Frequently asked questions


### What is the best free patent search tool?


Google Patents is a convenient free starting point for known documents, ordinary-language searching, and citation trails. Patent Public Search gives more control over advanced U.S. queries. Espacenet and PATENTSCOPE add international family, PCT, multilingual, classification, and chemical-search capabilities. A serious search often uses several of them.


### Is Google Patents enough for a prior art search?


Google Patents can support a strong first pass, but Google does not guarantee complete coverage. Its simple-family deduplication, approximate result counts, and top-1,000 CSV limit also shape what the reviewer sees. High-stakes work should use additional databases and the non-patent or factual sources relevant to the governing legal question.


### Can AI patent search replace Boolean search?


AI and Boolean search solve different retrieval problems. Semantic search helps when two sources express the same technical idea with different language. Boolean, field, proximity, classification, and date queries give the searcher exact controls and a reproducible syntax. A sound workflow uses semantic search to discover language, then structured searching to narrow and corroborate the result.


### Is a prior art search the same as an FTO search?


No. A prior art search asks whether qualifying earlier disclosures may affect patentability or validity under the governing law. A freedom-to-operate (FTO) search asks whether planned acts may fall within claims that are enforceable, or may become enforceable, in each country or region where the product will be made, used, sold, offered for sale, or imported. The analysis therefore turns on claim scope, relevant family members, ownership, term, and current legal status in each jurisdiction.


Published pending applications belong in the FTO review because they can mature into patents with claims that differ from the published claims. They are a future risk to monitor through prosecution, final abandonment, or grant. WIPO’s[FTO toolkit](https://www.wipo.int/tisc/en/docs/tisc-toolkit-freedom-to-operate-description.pdf) recommends searching both granted patents and published applications and checking each document’s current legal status.


Patentability and patent ownership still do not provide an affirmative right to practice an invention. A valid patent on an improvement can coexist with a broader blocking patent, because a patent grants a right to exclude rather than a right to commercialize. The USPTO explains that distinction in its guidance on the[nature of patent rights](https://www.uspto.gov/patents/basics/manage) .
